title: Semantic HTML
description: Structure meaningful documents: replace generic <div> containers with semantic landmarks (<header>, <nav>, <main>, <article>, <section>, <aside>, <footer>) that unlock accessibility, SEO, and maintainable architecture.

objectives.statement: Identify and use semantic landmark elements (header, nav, main, article, section, aside, footer) in place of generic div containers.
Evaluate architectural trade-offs between self-contained article elements and thematic section elements.

content.title: Beyond Div Soup
content.hook: To a visual browser, `<div>` and `<main>` might look identical until you add CSS. To a screen reader or search engine, they are the difference between an unnavigable maze and a structured document.
content.context: Semantic elements communicate intent. `<nav>` declares navigation, `<main>` declares primary content, `<article>` declares a self-contained syndicateable entity, and `<footer>` declares page metadata.
goals: Eliminate generic 'div soup' in favor of semantic landmarks.
Understand how semantic HTML forms the browser's Accessibility Tree.

content.title: The Semantic Landmark Map
content.description: Page layout: <header> contains <nav>. <main> contains <article> and <section>. <aside> contains supplementary sidebar. <footer> wraps bottom metadata. Each element generates a landmark in the Accessibility Tree.

content.title: Refactor the Div Soup
content.prompt: Refactor this non-semantic document. Replace `<div class="site-header">` with `<header>`, `<div class="main-nav">` with `<nav>`, `<div class="primary-content">` with `<main>`, and `<div class="site-footer">` with `<footer>`.

feedback.correct: Superb refactoring! You converted generic div containers into meaningful HTML5 accessibility landmarks.
feedback.incorrect: Make sure you used `<header>`, `<nav>`, `<main>`, and `<footer>` in place of the respective `<div>` elements.

content.title: Evaluate Semantic Structure Rubric
content.prompt: Evaluate whether a standalone blog post card on an index feed should be coded as an `<article>` or a generic `<div>` with styling classes.

modelAnswer.summary: The blog post card should be coded as an <article> element.
modelAnswer.detailedAnalysis: An <article> represents a self-contained composition in a document, page, application, or site, which is intended to be independently distributable or reusable (e.g., in syndication). A blog post card has its own heading, publication date, author, and content summary, making it an independent entity.
keyTradeoffs: <article> creates a discrete landmark and sectioning context in the Accessibility Tree.
<div> conveys no semantic meaning, forcing screen readers to treat the card as generic flow layout.
<section> is intended for thematic subsections of a larger work, whereas <article> is self-contained.

evaluationRubric.label: Self-Contained Syndicateable Unit
evaluationRubric.description: Identifies that <article> represents content that makes independent sense outside the page.

evaluationRubric.label: Accessibility Tree Landmarks
evaluationRubric.description: Explains the semantic and screen reader advantages over generic <div> wrappers.

content.prompt: How does substituting generic `<div>` elements with `<header>`, `<nav>`, `<main>`, and `<footer>` alter the Accessibility Tree generated by the browser for assistive screen readers?

feedback.correct: Outstanding! Semantic tags automatically expose standardized landmark roles (`banner`, `navigation`, `main`, `contentinfo`) in the Accessibility Tree, allowing screen reader users to jump directly between regions.
feedback.incorrect: Focus on how landmark roles are communicated to assistive technology and screen readers.

content.title: Key Takeaways: Semantic HTML
takeaways: Use semantic elements (`<header>`, `<nav>`, `<main>`, `<footer>`) to create landmark regions for assistive technology.
Use `<article>` for independent, standalone content; use `<section>` for thematic sub-divisions.
Reserve `<div>` solely for visual styling wrappers that have no semantic meaning.
Semantic HTML improves accessibility, search engine indexing, and code maintainability.
